Circle.explanation: A circle has no corners or edges and is perfectly round in every direction
points: All points on the circumference are exactly the same distance from the center (radius)
Has the maximum area for a given perimeter of any 2D shape
360 degrees or 2π radians — basis for angles and trigonometry
Never ends — infinite symmetry in every direction
Appears in nature (planets, ripples, eyes) due to equal force distribution

Square.explanation: A square has four equal sides and four right angles of exactly 90 degrees
points: All four sides and all four angles are perfectly equal
Diagonals are equal and bisect each other at 90 degrees
Most stable and space-efficient tiling shape for floors and grids
Symbol of stability, order, and equality in many cultures

Triangle.explanation: A triangle has three sides and the angles inside always add up to 180 degrees
points: Sum of interior angles is always exactly 180° (triangle angle theorem)
Strongest geometric shape — used in bridges, towers, and trusses
Types: equilateral (all equal), isosceles (two equal), scalene (all different)
Basis of trigonometry (sine, cosine, tangent functions)
Smallest polygon that can enclose area

Rectangle.explanation: A rectangle has four right angles but opposite sides are equal not all four
points: All angles are exactly 90° — opposite sides equal and parallel
Most common shape in human-made objects (screens, books, rooms)
Diagonals are equal and bisect each other
Special case: when length = width → becomes a square

Pentagon.explanation: A pentagon has five sides and five corners and is the shape of a home base in baseball
points: Regular pentagon has all sides and angles equal (108° interior angles)
Appears in nature (starfish, flowers) and architecture (Pentagon building)
Golden ratio (φ ≈ 1.618) is found in diagonals to side ratio
Cannot tile the plane by itself without gaps
Home plate in baseball is a regular pentagon with a triangle attached

Hexagon.explanation: A hexagon has six sides and honeybees build perfect hexagons in their hives
points: Most efficient shape for tiling plane with least perimeter (honeycomb proof)
Appears in snowflakes, benzene rings, and soccer ball panels
Can be divided into 6 equilateral triangles
Strong structural shape — used in nuts, bolts, and aerospace

Heptagon.explanation: A heptagon has seven sides and some coins like the British 50p use this shape
points: Regular heptagon cannot be constructed with compass and straightedge alone
British 50p and 20p coins are curved heptagons (constant width)
Appears in some viruses and architecture (heptagonal domes)
One of the most difficult regular polygons to draw accurately

Octagon.explanation: An octagon has eight sides and is the shape of a stop sign
points: Stop signs use octagon because it stands out from other road signs
Can be formed by cutting corners off a square
Used in UFC cage, architecture, and mirrors
Area formula involves side length and √(2 + √2)

Nonagon.explanation: A nonagon has nine sides and nine angles inside
points: Appears in some religious architecture and symbols
Cannot be constructed exactly with compass and straightedge
Used in some coin designs and decorative patterns
Nine-fold symmetry is rare in nature

Decagon.explanation: A decagon has ten equal sides and ten angles
points: Closely related to golden ratio and pentagon
Used in some dice (10-sided) and architecture
Can be constructed with compass and straightedge
Appears in some viruses and molecular structures

Oval.explanation: An oval is like a stretched circle and is also called an ellipse
points: Mathematically an ellipse — two focal points define the curve
No straight lines — smooth continuous curve
Used in racetracks, eggs, and sports stadiums
Area = π × a × b (a = semi-major, b = semi-minor axis)
Planetary orbits are ellipses (Kepler's first law)

Diamond.explanation: A diamond shape is a square turned 45 degrees on its corner
points: Also called rhombus when all sides equal
Common in playing cards, baseball fields, and jewelry cuts
Symbol of strength, clarity, and value

Star.explanation: A five-pointed star is called a pentagram and has been used in flags worldwide
points: Regular pentagram is a five-pointed star {5/2} Schläfli symbol
Used in flags (USA, China, Turkey, etc.) and mysticism
Can be drawn with one continuous line

Heart.explanation: The heart shape is a universal symbol of love used in all cultures
points: Stylized version of human heart — two lobes and point
Became romantic symbol in Middle Ages
Used in cards, emojis, tattoos, and branding
Mathematically can be approximated with cardioid curve
Almost universal across cultures for love and emotion

Crescent.explanation: A crescent is the shape of the Moon when it is partly lit by the Sun
points: Appears during waxing and waning Moon phases
Used in flags (Turkey, Pakistan, Malaysia, etc.) and symbols
Mathematically a lune — intersection of two circles
Symbol of growth, change, and Islam

Trapezoid.explanation: A trapezoid has one pair of parallel sides and is like a triangle with the top cut off
points: Exactly one pair of parallel sides (in American definition)
Median connects midpoints of non-parallel sides

Parallelogram.explanation: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides that lean to one side
points: Opposite angles equal; consecutive angles sum to 180°
Vectors AB and AD define the shape

Rhombus.explanation: A rhombus has four equal sides like a square but the angles are not 90 degrees
points: All four sides exactly equal length
Diagonals bisect each other at 90° and bisect vertex angles
Used in kites, diamonds, and some crystals

Sphere.explanation: A sphere is a perfectly round 3D ball where every point on the surface is equidistant
points: All points on surface equidistant from center (radius)
Maximum volume for given surface area of any 3D shape
Planets, stars, bubbles, and droplets are approximately spherical
Great circles are shortest paths on surface (geodesics)

Cube.explanation: A cube has six square faces twelve edges and eight corners all equal
points: Used in dice, Rubik’s cube, sugar cubes

Cylinder.explanation: A cylinder is like a can with two circular ends and one curved surface
points: Two parallel circular bases connected by curved surface
Used in engines, pipes, cans, columns
Right circular cylinder is most common

Cone.explanation: A cone has a circular base that narrows to a sharp point at the top
points: One circular base tapering to apex
Volume = (1/3)πr²h; surface area = πr(r + l) where l = slant height
Used in ice cream cones, party hats, volcanoes
Cross-sections are circles, ellipses, parabolas, hyperbolas
Conic section — formed by plane cutting cone

Pyramid.explanation: A pyramid has a square base and four triangular faces meeting at a point
points: Polygonal base with triangular faces to apex
Famous in Egypt (Great Pyramid of Giza)
Can have triangular, square, pentagonal bases, etc.
Used in architecture and crystal structures

Torus.explanation: A torus is the mathematical name for a donut shape with a hole in the middle
points: Surface of revolution of circle around axis
Used in physics (magnetic fields), architecture, and donuts
Can be embedded in 3D without self-intersection
Major radius (R) and minor radius (r) define size

Tetrahedron.explanation: A tetrahedron has four triangular faces and is the simplest 3D solid shape
points: Regular tetrahedron has all equilateral triangular faces
Strongest structural shape for minimal material

Octahedron.explanation: An octahedron has eight triangular faces and looks like two pyramids stuck together
points: Cross-section can be square, hexagon, triangle
Can be formed by two square pyramids joined at base

Dodecahedron.explanation: A dodecahedron has twelve pentagonal faces and is one of the five Platonic solids
points: Regular dodecahedron — 20 vertices, 12 pentagonal faces, 30 edges
Used in some dice (12-sided), cosmology models
Ancient Greek philosophers considered it symbol of cosmos

Icosahedron.explanation: An icosahedron has twenty triangular faces and looks like a fancy soccer ball
points: Regular icosahedron — 12 vertices, 20 triangular faces, 30 edges
Appears in viruses and geodesic domes

Prism.explanation: A prism has two identical parallel faces connected by rectangular sides
points: Two parallel congruent bases + rectangular lateral faces
Named by base: triangular prism, hexagonal prism, etc.
Used in optics, architecture, and packaging

Ellipsoid.explanation: An ellipsoid is like a stretched sphere such as the shape of a rugby ball
points: 3D version of ellipse — three axes (a, b, c)
Earth and planets are oblate spheroids (flattened at poles)
Used in geodesy, computer graphics, and design

Mobius Strip.explanation: A Mobius strip has only one surface and one edge and is impossible to paint both sides
points: One continuous edge and one surface
Cut lengthwise → becomes one longer loop
Used in conveyor belts, math topology, art
Discovered independently by Möbius and Listing in 1858

Helix.explanation: A helix is a three-dimensional spiral like a coiled spring or DNA strand
points: Used in springs, screws, DNA, staircases

Spiral.explanation: A spiral is a curve that moves away from a center point getting wider and wider
points: Golden spiral approximates logarithmic spiral with golden ratio
Used in art, architecture, and nature patterns

Fractal.explanation: Fractals are shapes that repeat the same pattern at every level of magnification
points: Self-similar — looks similar at any scale
Used in computer graphics, nature modeling, chaos theory
Coastline paradox — length increases with measurement scale

Parabola.explanation: A parabola is a U-shaped curve used in satellite dishes and headlights to focus beams
points: Defined as points equidistant from focus and directrix
Reflects parallel rays to focus (satellite dishes, headlights)
Appears in nature (water fountains, hanging chains ≈ catenary)

Hyperbola.explanation: A hyperbola is two mirror-image curved branches facing each other
points: Defined as points where difference of distances to two foci is constant
Used in navigation (LORAN), orbits, cooling towers
Conic section — plane cuts cone parallel to axis

Catenary.explanation: A catenary is the natural curve a hanging chain or cable makes under gravity
points: Stronger than parabola for load-bearing (arches, suspension bridges)
Gateway Arch in St. Louis is inverted catenary
Appears in spider webs, power lines

Cross.explanation: A cross shape is formed by two lines or rectangles intersecting at right angles
points: Most common forms: Latin cross, Greek cross, Celtic cross
Universal symbol in Christianity, medicine, flags
Can be rotated 45° to form diamond cross

Arrow.explanation: Arrow shapes point in a direction and have been used for navigation since ancient times
points: Consists of shaft, head (triangle), and sometimes fletching
Universal symbol for direction and motion
Used in signs, UI, flowcharts, archery
Ancient origins in hunting and warfare

Kite.explanation: A kite shape has two pairs of adjacent equal sides forming a bird-like diamond
points: Two pairs of adjacent equal sides
One pair of opposite angles equal
Used in kites, toys, and geometry
Special case of rhombus when all sides equal

Chevron.explanation: A chevron is a V-shaped zigzag pattern used in military ranks and road signs
points: Used in heraldry, military insignia, warning signs
Symbol of rank (more chevrons = higher rank)
Common in road markings (chevron alignment signs)

Trefoil.explanation: A trefoil is a three-lobed leaf shape used in architecture and as a symbol of the trinity
points: Symbol of Holy Trinity in Christianity
Appears in clover leaves and logos

Quatrefoil.explanation: A quatrefoil has four overlapping circles creating a four-leaf clover pattern
points: Common in Gothic and Renaissance architecture
Used in windows, tiles, and decorative patterns
Can be square or circular based

Vesica Piscis.explanation: A vesica piscis is formed by two overlapping circles with sacred geometric significance
points: Intersection of two circles of equal radius

Lemniscate.explanation: A lemniscate is the figure-eight infinity symbol that never ends
points: Used in mathematics, magic, and mysticism

Cardioid.explanation: A cardioid is a heart-shaped mathematical curve formed by a circle rolling around another
points: Generated by circle rolling around fixed circle
Used in acoustics, optics, and gear design

Reuleaux Triangle.explanation: A Reuleaux triangle is a curved triangle that rolls smoothly like a circle
points: Constant width — same diameter in every direction
Formed from intersection of three circles
Used in some rotary engines (Wankel) and drill bits
Not a true circle but has same width

Deltoid.explanation: A deltoid is a concave kite shape produced when a small circle rolls inside a larger one
points: Generated by circle rolling inside circle 3× radius
Used in some gear designs and math art

Astroid.explanation: An astroid is a four-pointed star shape with curved edges traced by a rolling circle
points: Generated by circle rolling inside 4× radius circle
Used in math, architecture, and jewelry
Has four cusps and diamond-like symmetry

Lune.explanation: A lune is a crescent-shaped region bounded by two arcs
points: Appears in Moon phases and flags
Can be used to square the circle (Hippocrates)

Annulus.explanation: An annulus is the ring-shaped region between two concentric circles
points: Used in washers, rings, and planetary rings
Appears in tree rings and growth patterns

Quadrant.explanation: A quadrant is one quarter of a circle like a pie slice cut at 90 degrees

Sector.explanation: A sector is a pie-slice portion of a circle between two radii
points: Area = (θ/360) × πr² or (θ/2) r² in radians
Used in pie charts, clocks, and fans

Segment.explanation: A segment is a region of a circle cut off by a straight chord
points: Appears in lenses and circular windows

Frustum.explanation: A frustum is a cone or pyramid with the top cut off creating a flat top surface
points: Used in buckets, lampshades, cooling towers

Bipyramid.explanation: A bipyramid is two pyramids joined at their square bases back to back
points: Can have triangular, pentagonal, etc. bases

Antiprism.explanation: An antiprism is like a prism but with one face rotated and triangles connecting the sides
points: Two parallel regular polygon bases rotated relative to each other

Prism Hexagonal.explanation: A hexagonal prism looks like a pencil before it is sharpened
points: Used in pencils, bolts, and crystals
Regular hexagonal prism has perfect hexagonal bases

Stellated Octahedron.explanation: A stellated octahedron looks like the Star of David in three dimensions

Klein Bottle.explanation: A Klein bottle is a one-sided surface with no inside or outside possible only in 4D
points: Non-orientable surface like Möbius strip but closed
Cannot be embedded in 3D without self-intersection

Hypercube.explanation: A hypercube or tesseract is the four-dimensional equivalent of a cube
points: 8 cubic cells, 24 square faces, 32 edges, 16 vertices
Projection to 3D looks like cube within cube
Used in physics (string theory), graphics, math

Penrose Triangle.explanation: The Penrose triangle is an impossible shape that cannot exist in three dimensions
points: Created by Oscar Reutersvärd (1934), popularized by Penrose
Used in Escher art and logos
Cannot be built in 3D without breaking

Golden Spiral.explanation: The golden spiral grows in proportion to the golden ratio and appears throughout nature
points: Logarithmic spiral with growth factor φ (≈1.618)
Appears in nautilus shells, galaxies, hurricanes
Related to golden ratio and Fibonacci sequence

Fibonacci Spiral.explanation: The Fibonacci spiral is based on Fibonacci numbers and matches the golden spiral closely
points: Quarter-circle arcs with radii following Fibonacci sequence
Appears in sunflower seeds, pinecones, pineapple
Used in art, design, and photography

Apollonius Circle.explanation: An Apollonius circle is defined by all points that maintain a fixed ratio of distances
points: Set of points with constant distance ratio to two fixed points
Used in geometry and inversive geometry
Special case: when ratio = 1 → perpendicular bisector
Important in circle packing and fractals

Epicycloid.explanation: An epicycloid is the path traced by a point on a circle rolling around another circle
points: Generated by circle rolling outside fixed circle
Used in gear design and math art

Hypocycloid.explanation: A hypocycloid is traced by a point on a small circle rolling inside a larger circle

Trochoid.explanation: A trochoid is the path traced by a point on a circle rolling along a straight line
points: Cycloid = point on rim, curtate cycloid = inside, prolate = outside
Used in gears, cams, and architecture
Generates arches and arches in buildings

Cycloid.explanation: A cycloid is the fastest sliding path between two points under gravity ignoring friction
points: Brachistochrone curve — fastest descent under gravity
Tautochrone — same travel time regardless of starting point
Generated by circle rolling on line

Archimedean Spiral.explanation: An Archimedean spiral grows by equal amounts for each turn unlike the golden spiral
points: Used in springs, records, and some galaxies

Fermat Spiral.explanation: A Fermat spiral grows so that each turn encloses equal area making it efficient in nature
points: Seeds in sunflowers follow Fermat spiral
Equal area per turn — efficient packing

Logarithmic Spiral.explanation: A logarithmic spiral maintains the same angle to its radius at every point
points: Constant angle to radius vector (equiangular spiral)
Self-similar — looks same at any scale
Appears in nautilus, galaxies, spider webs

Witch of Agnesi.explanation: The Witch of Agnesi is a bell-shaped curve with a funny name from a translation error
points: Used in probability, physics, and engineering

Sinusoidal Spiral.explanation: Sinusoidal spirals include shapes from circles to lemniscates depending on a single number
points: n=1 → cardioid, n=2 → lemniscate, n→∞ → circle
Used in math art and polar equations

Rose Curve.explanation: A rose curve is a beautiful petal-shaped mathematical curve created from a simple equation
points: Equation r = a cos(kθ) or sin(kθ)
k petals if k odd, 2k if k even
Used in art, design, and polar plots

Lissajous Figure.explanation: Lissajous figures are beautiful looping curves formed by two perpendicular oscillations
points: Parametric curve x = A sin(at + δ), y = B sin(bt)
Used in oscilloscopes and laser shows

Superellipse.explanation: A superellipse is the shape between an ellipse and a rectangle used in modern furniture design
points: Used in design (Piet Hein tables, stadiums)
Smooth transition between ellipse and rectangle

Stadion.explanation: A stadion is a rectangle with two semicircles on the ends like a running track shape
points: Also called capsule or racetrack shape
Used in running tracks, pills, stadiums

Reuleaux Polygon.explanation: Reuleaux polygons are shapes of constant width based on regular polygons
points: Constant width — same diameter in all directions
Used in rotary engines, coins, drill bits

Tensegrity.explanation: Tensegrity structures are made of floating compressed rods held together only by tension
points: Isolated components in compression, continuous tension

Polyhedron.explanation: A polyhedron is any solid 3D shape with flat faces straight edges and sharp vertices
points: Flat polygonal faces, straight edges, vertices
Convex vs concave vs star polyhedra
Euler characteristic V - E + F = 2 for convex

Zonohedron.explanation: A zonohedron is a convex polyhedron where every face is a parallelogram
points: Generated by Minkowski sum of line segments

Stellation.explanation: A stellation is made by extending a polyhedron's faces until they meet creating star shapes
points: Extending faces to form new polyhedra
Kepler-Poinsot polyhedra are stellations of Platonic solids
Can be infinite in some cases

Convex Hull.explanation: The convex hull is the smallest convex shape that contains a set of points like a rubber band stretched around pegs
points: Smallest convex set containing all points
Used in computer graphics, GIS, collision detection

Voronoi Cell.explanation: Voronoi cells divide space based on which seed point is nearest creating organic-looking patterns
points: Region closer to its seed than any other
Used in maps, art, robotics, biology
Appears in giraffe patterns, leaf cells

Penrose Tiling.explanation: Penrose tiles are two shapes that can tile a floor infinitely without ever repeating
points: Two rhombi (fat and thin) with matching rules

Squircle.explanation: A squircle is an intermediate shape between a square and a circle used in smartphone icons
points: Used in iOS icons, Samsung icons
Smoother than square, rounder than circle

Biangle.explanation: A biangle or digon has only two sides and two angles and exists on spherical geometry
points: Exists on sphere or hyperbolic plane

Hemicube.explanation: A hemicube is an abstract polyhedron made by identifying opposite faces of a cube
points: Three square faces meeting at each vertex
Abstract — cannot be realized in 3D without intersection

Flat Torus.explanation: A flat torus is a square where opposite edges are considered to be the same edge
points: Used in video games (Pac-Man screen wrap)

Manifold.explanation: A manifold is any shape that looks flat and normal when you zoom in very close
points: Examples: plane, sphere, torus, Klein bottle

Geodesic Dome.explanation: A geodesic dome is a spherical structure built from triangles invented by Buckminster Fuller
points: Very strong for weight — used in biospheres
Used in Epcot, radar stations, greenhouses

Frustum Cone.explanation: A conical frustum is the shape of a bucket or drinking cup wider at the top

Torus Knot.explanation: Torus knots are mathematical knots that wind around a torus surface like a twisted pretzel
points: Classified by (p,q) — winds p times one way, q the other
Used in math, art, and jewelry

Gyroid.explanation: A gyroid is a complex saddle-shaped periodic surface with no straight lines at all
points: Triply periodic — repeats in three directions
Found in butterfly wings and soap films
No straight lines or flat areas
Used in materials science and 3D printing

Schwarz Surface.explanation: Schwarz minimal surfaces are infinitely repeating soap-film-like mathematical surfaces
points: Schwarz P, D, H surfaces famous

Hyperboloid.explanation: A hyperboloid is a cooling tower shape made entirely from straight lines criss-crossing
points: Ruled surface — made of straight lines

Oloid.explanation: An oloid is a solid that rolls and wobbles unpredictably contacting its entire surface with the ground

Spindle Torus.explanation: A spindle torus is a torus where the tube is so fat it self-intersects at the center

Horn Torus.explanation: A horn torus is where the inner circle of a donut shape collapses to a single point
points: Looks like horn or apple shape
